lead: An FM receiver must turn frequency into voltage. The classic circuits do it in two steps: a tuned circuit turns the frequency swing into an amplitude or phase change, and diodes turn that into a voltage. One detuned tuned circuit gives the slope detector. Two balanced circuits do better. The Foster-Seeley discriminator uses a transformer whose secondary phase turns with frequency, and the ratio detector adds a large capacitor that gives it built-in limiting. These circuits fill the 10.7 MHz IF strips of older broadcast receivers; most newer chips use quadrature or digital detectors.
prereq: You need: the diode envelope detector (see AM demodulation: envelope and coherent detectors) and the FM wave (see Frequency and phase modulation concepts).

sections.h3: Slope detector: one detuned tuned circuit

blocks.text: A parallel tuned circuit's voltage peaks at its resonant frequency f<sub>r</sub> and falls away on both flanks. Tune f<sub>r</sub> a little to one side of the carrier f<sub>c</sub>, so the carrier sits on a flank. As the FM wave swings around f<sub>c</sub>, the tank voltage swings with it, and a diode envelope detector reads that voltage. Frequency deviation has become amplitude.
Q is the quality factor of the tank; f is the instantaneous frequency and f<sub>r</sub> the resonant frequency, both in Hz; the formula holds close to resonance.

Two faults. The flank is straight only over a small part of the bandwidth f<sub>r</sub>/Q, so a wide deviation is distorted (worked example 1). And the circuit is single-ended: any AM on the incoming wave, from noise or fading, passes straight to the audio, so a limiter must come first. A higher Q gives a steeper slope, more volts per kilohertz, but a shorter straight part.

The balanced slope detector uses one primary tuned to f<sub>c</sub> and two secondary tanks, one tuned above f<sub>c</sub> and one below, each with its own diode. The outputs are subtracted. The frequency effects have opposite signs and add, giving a steeper and straighter curve that is zero at f<sub>c</sub>; equal amplitude changes cancel. Its cost is alignment: the three tuned circuits must be trimmed against each other.

One transformer: the primary is tuned to f<sub>c</sub>, and the secondary is also tuned to f<sub>c</sub> and centre-tapped. A coupling capacitor and an RF choke put the primary voltage e<sub>p</sub> between the centre tap and the middle of the two diode loads. Each half of the secondary carries e<sub>s</sub>/2, the two halves in antiphase.

A tuned secondary driven through mutual inductance is 90° out of phase with the primary at resonance. Off resonance the angle changes: with e<sub>s</sub>/2 = j e<sub>p</sub> (k/(1 + jx)), where x = 2Q(f − f<sub>c</sub>)/f<sub>c</sub>, the angle is 90° − arctan x. Above f<sub>c</sub> it falls below 90°; below f<sub>c</sub> it rises above 90°. The secondary phase turns with frequency, and that is the mechanism.

Diode D1 sees the phasor sum e<sub>p</sub> + e<sub>s</sub>/2 and diode D2 sees e<sub>p</sub> − e<sub>s</sub>/2. Each diode with its RC load is an envelope detector, so V1 = |e<sub>p</sub> + e<sub>s</sub>/2| and V2 = |e<sub>p</sub> − e<sub>s</sub>/2|. The output is v<sub>o</sub> = V1 − V2. At f<sub>c</sub> the two sums have equal length and v<sub>o</sub> = 0. Above f<sub>c</sub>, V1 grows and V2 shrinks, so v<sub>o</sub> > 0; below f<sub>c</sub> the reverse. Plotted against frequency this is the S-curve, odd about f<sub>c</sub>, so the sign of the output says which side of f<sub>c</sub> the signal is on (Figure 3.4.1).

Near f<sub>c</sub> the secondary phase changes almost linearly with frequency, and near 90° the difference of the two lengths changes almost linearly with the phase; one nearly linear law applied after the other gives a wide straight region. Both V1 and V2 scale with the input amplitude, so at f<sub>c</sub> an amplitude change cancels, but away from f<sub>c</sub> it does not: a limiter still goes before the Foster-Seeley. An integrator after the output turns the same circuit into a PM detector.

sections.h3: Ratio detector, and the family compared

blocks.text: Turn one diode round and connect a large capacitor C across both loads. Now the diodes charge C to V1 + V2, not V1 − V2, and the audio is taken between the load midpoint and the capacitor midpoint, giving (V1 − V2)/2. The time constant of C with the loads is long, many audio cycles, so V1 + V2 is held almost constant. A sudden rise in input amplitude tries to raise both voltages; the capacitor soaks it up, and the output, which now depends only on the ratio V1/V2, follows frequency alone.

That is the built-in limiting, and many receivers use the ratio detector with only a light limiter or none. The price: half the output of a Foster-Seeley for the same input, limiting that fails for fast or deep amplitude changes, and diodes that must be matched.

examples.question: A slope detector for a 455 kHz narrowband FM signal with ±5 kHz deviation uses a tank tuned to f<sub>r</sub> = 465 kHz with Q = 50, driven at 1 V peak at resonance. Find the tank voltage at f<sub>c</sub> and at the two frequency extremes, and comment on linearity.
steps: Bandwidth f<sub>r</sub>/Q = 465/50 = 9.3 kHz; the carrier sits 10 kHz below f<sub>r</sub>, on the lower flank.
The positive swing is about twice the negative one, so the audio is badly distorted. The straight part of the flank is much narrower than ±5 kHz here; a lower Q or a balanced detector is needed.
examples.answer: Tank voltage 0.422 V at f<sub>c</sub>, 0.681 V at 460 kHz and 0.296 V at 450 kHz: swings of +0.259 and −0.126 V, so a single slope detector distorts even ±5 kHz.

examples.question: A Foster-Seeley discriminator at 10.7 MHz has e<sub>p</sub> = 1 V and |e<sub>s</sub>/2| = 1 V at f<sub>c</sub>, with secondary Q = 20. Find V1, V2 and v<sub>o</sub> at f<sub>c</sub>, at f<sub>c</sub> + 50 kHz and at f<sub>c</sub> − 50 kHz. What would a ratio detector give at +50 kHz?
steps: At f<sub>c</sub>: e<sub>s</sub>/2 = j1 V, so V1 = V2 = |1 + j| = 1.414 V and v<sub>o</sub> = 0.
At −50 kHz the angle is 100.6°, so V1 = 1.267 V and V2 = 1.526 V: v<sub>o</sub> = −0.259 V, the same size with the sign reversed.
Ratio detector at +50 kHz: (V1 − V2)/2 = 0.129 V, half the Foster-Seeley output, while V1 + V2 = 2.79 V stays close to its 2.83 V value at f<sub>c</sub>.
examples.answer: v<sub>o</sub> = 0 at f<sub>c</sub> and ±0.259 V at ±50 kHz (V1 = 1.526 V, V2 = 1.267 V); the ratio detector gives 0.129 V.

traps: A single slope detector's output is not zero at the carrier: it sits at a bias point on the flank. The balanced slope, Foster-Seeley and ratio detectors give zero at f<sub>c</sub>.
The S-curve is straight only over a limited range; beyond its peaks (±328 kHz in worked example 2) the output falls again, so more deviation does not give more output.
The Foster-Seeley secondary is tuned to f<sub>c</sub>, the same as the primary. The 90° comes from the tuned secondary, not from detuning.
The ratio detector limits only slow or moderate amplitude changes. Do not write that it removes all AM.

quiz.q: What does the limiter before an FM detector do, and why is it needed?
quiz.a: It clips away amplitude changes caused by noise and fading and delivers a constant-amplitude wave, so the detector responds to frequency only. Without it a slope or Foster-Seeley detector would pass AM to the audio.

quiz.q: Why is the Foster-Seeley circuit called a phase discriminator?
quiz.a: Its diodes compare the phase of the secondary voltage with the primary voltage, and that phase changes with frequency, so the output measures the frequency offset.

quiz.q: Why must the carrier of a slope detector sit on the straight part of the tank curve?
quiz.a: The output is slope × deviation only where the slope is constant. On the curved part equal frequency steps give unequal voltage steps, and the audio is distorted.

quiz.q: How does a balanced slope detector reduce AM at its output?
quiz.a: Two secondary tanks sit on opposite sides of f<sub>c</sub>, each with a diode, and their outputs are subtracted. An amplitude change raises both outputs equally and cancels; a frequency change raises one and lowers the other, so the frequency effects add.

quiz.q: A Foster-Seeley discriminator gives +2.4 V at +40 kHz deviation and is linear in that range. What deviation gives −1.2 V?
quiz.a: Ratio −1.2/2.4 = −0.5, so the deviation is −0.5 × 40 = −20 kHz.

quiz.q: Explain why the ratio detector gives about half the output of a Foster-Seeley and what it gains in return.
quiz.a: Its output is taken as (V1 − V2)/2 between the load midpoint and the capacitor midpoint, half the Foster-Seeley V1 − V2. In return the large capacitor holds V1 + V2 nearly constant, so the output follows only the ratio V1/V2 and slow amplitude changes are rejected inside the detector.

beyond: Not for the exam. Newer receivers sample the IF as I and Q values and compute the phase with an arctangent; the change of phase from one sample to the next is the frequency. This polar discriminator is the Foster-Seeley idea done in arithmetic, and it is what software-defined radios use. Many analog FM chips use a quadrature detector instead, a phase-shift network and a multiplier. Search for quadrature FM detector and polar discriminator.
